summary: Provides a framework for translating between IPv4 and IPv6, in the context of replacing NAT-PT (deprecated by RFC 4966) and letting both coexist during the move to IPv6. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes ways to translate packets and addresses between IPv4 and IPv6 networks. It compares situations where translation can help and explains why it is a coexistence tool rather than a complete transition plan.

subtitle: A framework for choosing IPv4/IPv6 translation approaches during network coexistence and transition.

tldr.problem: Networks moving from IPv4 to IPv6 may still need communication between systems that support different address families. NAT-PT had operational problems and was deprecated.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lays out eight communication scenarios and a framework involving address translation, packet-header translation, state, DNS translation, and application-layer gateways. It compares stateless and stateful translation.
tldr.outcome: The document recommends translation as a medium-term coexistence tool rather than a long-term transition plan. Companion specifications define individual parts of the framework.

today: RFC 6144 is an Informational RFC published in April 2011, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The framework points to RFC 6052, RFC 6145, RFC 6146, and RFC 6147 for component specifications.

sections.title: Why Translate Between IPv4 and IPv6
sections.content:
This framework addresses coexistence between IPv4 and IPv6 while networks move toward IPv6. It was written in the context of replacing NAT-PT, which was deprecated because of operational issues and was not considered a viable medium- or long-term general-purpose strategy.

The RFC describes translation as one tool for cases where dual-stack deployment or tunneling is not sufficient. It characterizes translation as a medium-term coexistence strategy that can help a longer-term transition.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv4 and IPv6 systems may need to communicate during a transition period. Translation is one tool for that period, but the RFC does not present it as a permanent solution.

sections.title: Eight Translation Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC divides translation into four settings: an IPv6 network and the IPv4 Internet, an IPv4 network and the IPv6 Internet, an IPv6 network and an IPv4 network, and the two Internets. Each setting has two scenarios depending on which side starts communication, for eight scenarios total.

The RFC says an IPv6 network reaching the IPv4 Internet can use either stateful or stateless translation. The two whole-Internet scenarios have no viable method for unlimited translation because the address spaces differ greatly. Some other settings are described as difficult or as needing only a subset of the possible addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The appropriate translation method depends on which kind of network is communicating and which side starts. The framework describes eight such cases and notes that some are harder than others.

sections.title: Components of the Framework
sections.content:
The framework includes address translation, IP and ICMP translation, translation-state maintenance, DNS64 and DNS46, and application-layer gateways for protocols that need special handling. The address mapping rules are described in RFC 6052, packet-header translation in RFC 6145, stateful translation in RFC 6146, and DNS64 in RFC 6147.

DNS64 can translate an A record into a AAAA record, while DNS46 is described as translating a AAAA record into an A record. The preferred behavior is to synthesize a record only when no reachable record of the needed type exists. Some applications may also require an application-layer gateway, with FTP given as an example.
sections.plainLanguage: Translation needs more than changing an address. The framework also covers packet headers, connection state, DNS answers, and special handling for applications that need it.

sections.title: Stateless and Stateful Translation
sections.content:
Stateless translation derives mapping information from the address and configured information. It can support connections started from either side, supports end-to-end address transparency, and can be used in scenarios 1, 2, 5, and 6. It constrains which IPv6 addresses can be assigned to nodes using the mapping.

Stateful translation keeps dynamic mappings between IPv4 and IPv6 address and port information. It can be used in scenarios 1, 3, and 5, and generally supports communication initiated from the IPv6 side. The RFC notes that dynamically bound addresses are not stable IPv6 addresses for DNS use.
sections.plainLanguage: A stateless translator follows configured address rules and can support sessions started from either side, but it limits address choices. A stateful translator keeps temporary mappings and generally supports sessions started from IPv6.

sections.title: Use, Security and Open Problems
sections.content:
The RFC recommends temporary use of translation while IPv6 services are brought up elsewhere in a network, followed by removing unnecessary IPv4 service when conditions warrant. It describes coexistence with IPv4 and IPv6 hosts, applications, and networks.

The framework does not cover every possible scenario and may be extended. It defines no translation protocol itself; the security issues are addressed in the individual specifications for address translation, packet translation, state, DNS64, and application support.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC recommends using translation to bridge parts of a network while IPv6 is deployed. It is a framework, so details and security issues belong to the specifications for each component.
